claim: Mushroom bodies are the iconic learning and memory centers of insects.
source: Mushroom bodies are the iconic learning and memory centers of insects.
evidence: This is a well-established characterization in the field, supported by extensive research cited throughout the manuscript.

claim: No previously described crustacean possesses a mushroom body as defined by strict morphological criteria.
source: No previously described crustacean possesses a mushroom body as defined by strict morphological criteria although crustacean centers called hemiellipsoid bodies, which serve functions in sensory integration, have been viewed as evolutionarily convergent with mushroom bodies.
evidence: This claim is based on a review of existing literature on crustacean neuroanatomy.

claim: Crustacean centers called hemiellipsoid bodies serve functions in sensory integration.
source: No previously described crustacean possesses a mushroom body as defined by strict morphological criteria although crustacean centers called hemiellipsoid bodies, which serve functions in sensory integration, have been viewed as evolutionarily convergent with mushroom bodies.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research on hemiellipsoid bodies.

claim: Hemiellipsoid bodies have been viewed as evolutionarily convergent with mushroom bodies.
source: No previously described crustacean possesses a mushroom body as defined by strict morphological criteria although crustacean centers called hemiellipsoid bodies, which serve functions in sensory integration, have been viewed as evolutionarily convergent with mushroom bodies.
evidence: This reflects a historical interpretation in the literature.

claim: Stomatopod crustaceans (mantis shrimps) possess insect-like mushroom bodies.
source: Here, using key identifiers to characterize neural arrangements, we demonstrate insect-like mushroom bodies in stomatopod crustaceans (mantis shrimps).
evidence: This is the primary finding of the study, supported by extensive neuroanatomical data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Mantis shrimps display sophisticated behaviors relating to predation, spatial memory, and visual recognition comparable to those of insects.
source: More than any other crustacean taxon, mantis shrimps display sophisticated behaviors relating to predation, spatial memory, and visual recognition comparable to those of insects.
evidence: This is supported by citations to behavioral studies on mantis shrimps.

claim: Neuroanatomy-based cladistics suggests close phylogenetic proximity of insects and stomatopod crustaceans.
source: However, neuroanatomy-based cladistics suggesting close phylogenetic proximity of insects and stomatopod crustaceans conflicts with genomic evidence showing hexapods closely related to simple crustaceans called remipedes.
evidence: This is based on morphological comparisons and neural cladistics approaches.

claim: Genomic evidence shows hexapods closely related to simple crustaceans called remipedes.
source: However, neuroanatomy-based cladistics suggesting close phylogenetic proximity of insects and stomatopod crustaceans conflicts with genomic evidence showing hexapods closely related to simple crustaceans called remipedes.
evidence: This is supported by multiple molecular phylogenetic studies cited in the manuscript.

claim: There is a conflict between neuroanatomy-based cladistics and genomic evidence regarding insect-crustacean relationships.
source: However, neuroanatomy-based cladistics suggesting close phylogenetic proximity of insects and stomatopod crustaceans conflicts with genomic evidence showing hexapods closely related to simple crustaceans called remipedes.
evidence: This conflict is a central theme of the discussion in the manuscript.

claim: Mushroom bodies were first identified in the brains of Hymenoptera by Dujardin in 1850.
source: Mushroom bodies are paired centers first identified in the brains of Hymenoptera (Dujardin, 1850).
evidence: This is a historical fact supported by citation.

claim: Mushroom bodies are anatomically defined as a discrete neuropil composed of an abundance of parallel fibers originating from densely packed cell bodies called globuli cells or Kenyon cells.
source: They have been defined anatomically as a discrete neuropil composed of an abundance of parallel fibers originating from densely packed cell bodies, called globuli cells or Kenyon cells (Schürmann F-W, 1973).
evidence: This is a standard anatomical definition supported by citation.

claim: The parallel fibers of mushroom bodies form a distinctive peduncle that divides into two or more columnar tributaries termed lobes.
source: Together, the parallel fibers form a distinctive peduncle that divides into two or more columnar tributaries termed lobes.
evidence: This is part of the standard anatomical description of mushroom bodies.

claim: Input and output neurons intersect parallel fibers down the length of each lobe, partitioning the lobe into discrete territories.
source: Input and output neurons intersect parallel fibers down the length of each lobe, partitioning the lobe into discrete territories (Mobbs, 1982; Li and Strausfeld, 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous anatomical studies.

claim: In most neopteran insects, parallel fibers provide systems of dendrites that form a distal cap- or cup-like domain called the calyx.
source: In most neopteran insects (those insects possessing wings that bend over the abdomen), parallel fibers provide systems of dendrites that form a distal cap- or cup-like domain called the calyx that receives afferents from olfactory neuropils and, in many species, from the optic lobes and gustatory centers as well.
evidence: This is a well-established anatomical feature of neopteran insect mushroom bodies.

claim: The calyx receives afferents from olfactory neuropils and, in many species, from the optic lobes and gustatory centers.
source: In most neopteran insects (those insects possessing wings that bend over the abdomen), parallel fibers provide systems of dendrites that form a distal cap- or cup-like domain called the calyx that receives afferents from olfactory neuropils and, in many species, from the optic lobes and gustatory centers as well.
evidence: This describes the sensory inputs to the mushroom body calyx.

claim: Calyces are absent in palaeopteran insects, such as odonates and Ephemeroptera (dragonflies, darters, mayflies).
source: Calyces are absent in palaeopteran insects, such as odonates and Ephemeroptera (dragonflies, darters, mayflies), as well as in secondarily aquatic Neoptera such as diving beetles (Strausfeld et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a comparative study.

claim: Calyces are absent in secondarily aquatic Neoptera such as diving beetles.
source: Calyces are absent in palaeopteran insects, such as odonates and Ephemeroptera (dragonflies, darters, mayflies), as well as in secondarily aquatic Neoptera such as diving beetles (Strausfeld et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a comparative study.

claim: Mushroom bodies include the presence of inhibitory feedback pathways from proximal to more distal levels of the lobes and calyx.
source: Additional characters conventionally attributed to mushroom bodies include the presence of inhibitory feedback pathways from proximal to more distal levels of the lobes and calyx (Leitch and Laurent, 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a study on mushroom body circuitry.

claim: Mushroom bodies are defined by enriched expression of proteins that are known to be essential for learning and memory functions in Drosophila.
source: Mushroom bodies are further defined by enriched expression of proteins that are known to be essential for learning and memory functions in Drosophila (Skoulakis et al., 1993; Skoulakis and Davis, 1996; Wang et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to molecular studies in Drosophila.

claim: The exclusive location of the paired mushroom bodies is laterally in the protocerebrum (forebrain).
source: The exclusive location of the paired mushroom bodies is laterally in the protocerebrum (forebrain), as they are in another mandibulate group, Myriapoda, which includes centipedes and millipedes (Wolff and Strausfeld, 2015).
evidence: This describes the anatomical location of mushroom bodies, supported by citation.

claim: Mushroom bodies are located laterally in the protocerebrum in Myriapoda, which includes centipedes and millipedes.
source: The exclusive location of the paired mushroom bodies is laterally in the protocerebrum (forebrain), as they are in another mandibulate group, Myriapoda, which includes centipedes and millipedes (Wolff and Strausfeld, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a comparative study.

claim: Mushroom body function has been attributed to learning and memory.
source: Mushroom body function has been attributed to learning and memory (Heisenberg, 2003).
evidence: This is a well-established functional characterization supported by citation.

claim: Convergence of populations of relay neurons from the antennal lobes onto sparse subsets of mushroom body Kenyon cells underlies multiple representations of odors.
source: Currently, much of our knowledge about the roles of mushroom bodies comes from studies showing that convergence of populations of relay neurons from the antennal lobes onto sparse subsets of mushroom body Kenyon cells underlies multiple representations of odors (Campbell et al., 2013; Perez-Orive et al., 2002; Lin et al., 2014); that mushroom bodies mediate appetitive and aversive long-term memory (Waddell, 2013); and that they support allocentric and sequential place memory such as during trap-line foraging and obligate parasitoidism (Mizunami et al., 1998; Montgomery et al., 2016; Farris and Schulmeister, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies on mushroom body function.

claim: Mushroom bodies mediate appetitive and aversive long-term memory.
source: Currently, much of our knowledge about the roles of mushroom bodies comes from studies showing that convergence of populations of relay neurons from the antennal lobes onto sparse subsets of mushroom body Kenyon cells underlies multiple representations of odors (Campbell et al., 2013; Perez-Orive et al., 2002; Lin et al., 2014); that mushroom bodies mediate appetitive and aversive long-term memory (Waddell, 2013); and that they support allocentric and sequential place memory such as during trap-line foraging and obligate parasitoidism (Mizunami et al., 1998; Montgomery et al., 2016; Farris and Schulmeister, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a review on mushroom body function.

claim: Mushroom bodies support allocentric and sequential place memory such as during trap-line foraging and obligate parasitoidism.
source: Currently, much of our knowledge about the roles of mushroom bodies comes from studies showing that convergence of populations of relay neurons from the antennal lobes onto sparse subsets of mushroom body Kenyon cells underlies multiple representations of odors (Campbell et al., 2013; Perez-Orive et al., 2002; Lin et al., 2014); that mushroom bodies mediate appetitive and aversive long-term memory (Waddell, 2013); and that they support allocentric and sequential place memory such as during trap-line foraging and obligate parasitoidism (Mizunami et al., 1998; Montgomery et al., 2016; Farris and Schulmeister, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on spatial memory and behavior.

claim: Mushroom bodies have been identified in Myriapoda (centipedes and millipedes).
source: Given that mushroom bodies have been identified in Myriapoda (centipedes and millipedes) and Chelicerata (arachnids, horseshoe crabs, and sea spiders) (Wolff and Strausfeld, 2015), it might be assumed that these centers would be ubiquitous across arthropods.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a comparative study.

claim: Mushroom bodies have been identified in Chelicerata (arachnids, horseshoe crabs, and sea spiders).
source: Given that mushroom bodies have been identified in Myriapoda (centipedes and millipedes) and Chelicerata (arachnids, horseshoe crabs, and sea spiders) (Wolff and Strausfeld, 2015), it might be assumed that these centers would be ubiquitous across arthropods.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a comparative study.

claim: The paired higher centers in the lateral protocerebrum of crustaceans share few, if any, of the identifying characteristics of lobed mushroom bodies.
source: However, that assumption is awkward because the paired higher centers in the lateral protocerebrum of crustaceans share few, if any, of the identifying characteristics of lobed mushroom bodies as described above.
evidence: This is based on comparative neuroanatomical observations.

claim: The paired higher centers in the lateral protocerebrum of crustaceans are the domed hemiellipsoid bodies.
source: However, that assumption is awkward because the paired higher centers in the lateral protocerebrum of crustaceans share few, if any, of the identifying characteristics of lobed mushroom bodies as described above. These paired centers are the domed hemiellipsoid bodies.
evidence: This is a standard anatomical identification in crustacean neurobiology.

claim: In malacostracan crustaceans, such as crayfish and shrimps, hemiellipsoid bodies may correspond functionally to mushroom bodies.
source: Particularly in malacostracan crustaceans, such as crayfish and shrimps, hemiellipsoid bodies may correspond functionally to mushroom bodies.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on functional similarities.

claim: In many species the hemiellipsoid bodies are subdivided into discrete lateral domains and levels.
source: In many species the hemiellipsoid bodies are subdivided into discrete lateral domains and levels (Sullivan and Beltz, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a comparative study.

claim: Hemiellipsoid body neurons originate from a dense population of minute cell bodies situated at the dorsal and dorsolateral surfaces of the lateral protocerebra.
source: Their neurons originate from a dense population of minute cell bodies situated at the dorsal and dorsolateral surfaces of the lateral protocerebra, like the perikarya of globuli cells associated with the insect mushroom body.
evidence: This is a comparative anatomical observation.

claim: Only in one group of crustaceans, the Anomura (hermit crabs), has there been any description of enriched proteins involved in learning and memory that characterize insect mushroom body lobes.
source: However, only in one group of crustaceans, the Anomura (hermit crabs), has there been any description of enriched proteins involved in learning and memory that characterize insect mushroom body lobes.
evidence: This is based on a review of the literature on crustacean neurochemistry.

claim: In the land hermit crab Coenobita clypeatus, learning and memory proteins are confined to discrete concentric layers arranged at intervals through the depth of the hemiellipsoid body.
source: In the land hermit crab Coenobita clypeatus, these proteins are confined to discrete concentric layers arranged at intervals through the depth of the hemiellipsoid body.
evidence: This is based on immunocytological observations.

claim: Planar arrangements of pre- and postsynaptic neurons in the hemiellipsoid body strata of Coenobita clypeatus are comparable to orthogonal networks observed in the mushroom body lobes of insects.
source: Planar arrangements of pre- and postsynaptic neurons in these strata are comparable to orthogonal networks observed in the mushroom body lobes of insects.
evidence: This is a comparative anatomical observation.

claim: The hemiellipsoid bodies of land hermit crabs are interpreted as homologues of insect mushroom bodies.
source: Hence, the hemiellipsoid bodies of land hermit crabs are interpreted as homologues of insect mushroom bodies (Brown and Wolff, 2012).
evidence: This is an interpretation based on anatomical and molecular similarities, supported by citation.

claim: Marine hermit crabs show no evidence of orthogonal circuitry in their hemiellipsoid bodies.
source: But the question remains whether such circuits have evolved convergently, particularly because marine hermit crabs show no evidence of orthogonal circuitry, nor do species of the related orders, Astacidea (crayfish and lobsters) and Brachyura (true crabs).
evidence: This is based on comparative neuroanatomical observations.

claim: Species of the orders Astacidea (crayfish and lobsters) and Brachyura (true crabs) show no evidence of orthogonal circuitry in their hemiellipsoid bodies.
source: But the question remains whether such circuits have evolved convergently, particularly because marine hermit crabs show no evidence of orthogonal circuitry, nor do species of the related orders, Astacidea (crayfish and lobsters) and Brachyura (true crabs).
evidence: This is based on comparative neuroanatomical observations.

claim: Stomatopoda (mantis shrimps) is the sister group of all eumalacostracan crustaceans.
source: Stomatopoda (mantis shrimps), which is the sister group of all eumalacostracan crustaceans (Wolfe et al., 2016), engage in such behaviors.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a phylogenetic study.

claim: Stomatopods possess the most elaborate visual systems of any arthropod.
source: Stomatopods possess the most elaborate visual systems of any arthropod, where each eye moves independently of the other, and is endowed with binocular vision and numerous color- and polarization-sensitive channels, including channels for detecting circular polarization (Marshall et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a study on stomatopod vision.

claim: Each stomatopod eye moves independently of the other.
source: Stomatopods possess the most elaborate visual systems of any arthropod, where each eye moves independently of the other, and is endowed with binocular vision and numerous color- and polarization-sensitive channels, including channels for detecting circular polarization (Marshall et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a known feature of stomatopod vision, supported by citation.

claim: Stomatopod eyes are endowed with binocular vision and numerous color- and polarization-sensitive channels, including channels for detecting circular polarization.
source: Stomatopods possess the most elaborate visual systems of any arthropod, where each eye moves independently of the other, and is endowed with binocular vision and numerous color- and polarization-sensitive channels, including channels for detecting circular polarization (Marshall et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a study on stomatopod vision.

claim: Mantis shrimps frequent established hunting territories distant from their lair.
source: Mantis shrimps frequent established hunting territories distant from their lair (Cronin et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a behavioral study.

claim: Mantis shrimps form associative memories of kin and place through sensory integration employing the modalities of vision and olfaction.
source: Like insects, mantis shrimps form associative memories of kin and place through sensory integration employing the modalities of vision and olfaction (Caldwell and Lamp, 1981) and can be trained in discrimination-learning paradigms using color and polarized light stimuli (Marshall et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to behavioral studies.

claim: Mantis shrimps can be trained in discrimination-learning paradigms using color and polarized light stimuli.
source: Like insects, mantis shrimps form associative memories of kin and place through sensory integration employing the modalities of vision and olfaction (Caldwell and Lamp, 1981) and can be trained in discrimination-learning paradigms using color and polarized light stimuli (Marshall et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a behavioral study.

claim: Individual mantis shrimps remember conspecifics with which they have had aversive or non-aversive encounters.
source: Individuals remember conspecifics with which they have had aversive or non-aversive encounters (Caldwell, 1992).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a behavioral study.

claim: The behaviors of mantis shrimps require a brain equipped for memory of places, territories and individual recognition.
source: These behaviors require a brain equipped for memory of places, territories and individual recognition (Marshall et al., 1996).
evidence: This is an inference based on behavioral observations, supported by citation.

claim: Similarity of brain structures has suggested phylogenetic proximity of insects and malacostracan crustaceans.
source: Their similarity of brain structures has suggested phylogenetic proximity of insects and malacostracan crustaceans (Strausfeld and Andrew, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a neuroanatomical cladistics study.

claim: Genomic evidence argues strongly that insects are most closely related to blind, morphologically simple cave-dwelling crustaceans, called remipedes.
source: However, genomic evidence argues strongly that insects are instead most closely related to blind, morphologically simple cave-dwelling crustaceans, called remipedes (Regier et al., 2005; Oakley et al., 2013; von Reumont et al., 2012; Schwentner et al., 2017), which like all crustaceans other than stomatopods lack mushroom bodies.
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple molecular phylogenetic studies.

claim: All crustaceans other than stomatopods lack mushroom bodies.
source: However, genomic evidence argues strongly that insects are instead most closely related to blind, morphologically simple cave-dwelling crustaceans, called remipedes (Regier et al., 2005; Oakley et al., 2013; von Reumont et al., 2012; Schwentner et al., 2017), which like all crustaceans other than stomatopods lack mushroom bodies.
evidence: This is a claim based on the findings of the current study and review of literature.

claim: Within more recently radiating eumalacostracan lineages, the neuronal composition and organization of mushroom body morphology appear to have undergone radical modification resulting in centers unrecognizable as mushroom bodies but retaining the function of a sensory integrator.
source: We show that, within more recently radiating eumalacostracan lineages, the neuronal composition and organization of mushroom body morphology appear to have undergone radical modification resulting in centers unrecognizable as mushroom bodies but retaining the function of a sensory integrator.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on comparative neuroanatomical data presented in the study.

claim: A hexapod-malacostracan-like brain has been identified in a fossil stem arthropod.
source: The earlier identification of a hexapod-malacostracan-like brain in a fossil stem arthropod (Ma et al., 2015) together with the present results argues for an elaborate ancestral cerebral organization already present in the lower Cambrian.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a paleontological study.

claim: An elaborate ancestral cerebral organization was already present in the lower Cambrian.
source: The earlier identification of a hexapod-malacostracan-like brain in a fossil stem arthropod (Ma et al., 2015) together with the present results argues for an elaborate ancestral cerebral organization already present in the lower Cambrian.
evidence: This is an inference based on fossil evidence and the current findings.

claim: In stomatopods, the brain's lateral protocerebra are contained within the distal eyestalks.
source: In stomatopods, as in most stalk-eyed crustaceans, the brain's lateral protocerebra are contained within the distal eyestalks (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a direct anatomical observation supported by Figure 1C.

claim: The lateral protocerebra in mantis shrimps are exceptionally capacious due to the voluminous nested optic lobe neuropils.
source: These are exceptionally capacious in mantis shrimps due to the voluminous nested optic lobe neuropils, which serve the largest and most complex compound eyes yet described (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a direct anatomical observation supported by Figure 1A.

claim: Mantis shrimps have the largest and most complex compound eyes yet described.
source: These are exceptionally capacious in mantis shrimps due to the voluminous nested optic lobe neuropils, which serve the largest and most complex compound eyes yet described (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by the image in Figure 1A and is consistent with known literature on stomatopod vision.

claim: In the mantis shrimp, the largest neuropil of the lateral protocerebrum originates from a dorsal cell body cluster of about 170,000 minute and tightly clustered neuronal perikarya.
source: In the mantis shrimp, the largest of these neuropils originates from a dorsal cell body cluster of about 170,000 (in N. oerstedii) minute and tightly clustered neuronal perikarya, which we here refer to as globuli cells.
evidence: This is based on cell counts from the study.

claim: The globuli cell population in mantis shrimps provides the neurons that form four columnar neuropils, each comprising thousands of parallel fibers.
source: This population provides the neurons that form four columnar neuropils, each comprising thousands of parallel fibers.
evidence: This is a direct anatomical observation from the study.

claim: Only one of the four columns in mantis shrimps is surmounted by a large calyx-like neuropil.
source: Only one of the four columns is surmounted by a large calyx-like neuropil (Figure 1D) composed of layers of dendritic arborizations.
evidence: This is a direct anatomical observation supported by Figure 1D.

claim: The large calyx-like neuropil in mantis shrimps is composed of layers of dendritic arborizations.
source: Only one of the four columns is surmounted by a large calyx-like neuropil (Figure 1D) composed of layers of dendritic arborizations.
evidence: This is a direct anatomical observation supported by Figure 1D.

claim: The four columns in mantis shrimps extend latero-caudally and together demarcate the proximal margin of the eyestalk neuropil, near its junction with the eyestalk nerve.
source: The four columns (Figure 1E), which extend latero-caudally, together demarcate the proximal margin of the eyestalk neuropil, near its junction with the eyestalk nerve (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a direct anatomical observation supported by Figures 1C and 1E.

claim: Globuli cells in mantis shrimps provide one very large dome-like neuropil (calyx) from which one of the smaller columns originates.
source: Globuli cells provide one very large dome-like neuropil (here termed the calyx, indicated Ca in Figure 1D,E) from which one of the smaller columns originates (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is a direct anatomical observation supported by figures.

claim: Globuli cells in mantis shrimps also provide parallel fibers constituting three additional columns.
source: Globuli cells also provide parallel fibers constituting three additional columns (Figure 1E; Figure 2B,C), one of which is equipped with a small calyx distally (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is a direct anatomical observation supported by figures.

claim: One of the three additional columns in mantis shrimps is equipped with a small calyx distally.
source: Globuli cells also provide parallel fibers constituting three additional columns (Figure 1E; Figure 2B,C), one of which is equipped with a small calyx distally (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is a direct anatomical observation supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 3B.

claim: Two of the columns in mantis shrimps lack distal dendrites entirely.
source: The two other columns lack distal dendrites entirely.
evidence: This is a direct anatomical observation from the study.

claim: Neurites from globuli cells converge at the origin of each column in mantis shrimps, as they do at the pedunculus of an insect mushroom body.
source: Neurites from globuli cells converge at the origin of each column, as they do at the pedunculus (or initial stalk) of an insect mushroom body (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A,B).
evidence: This is a comparative anatomical observation supported by figures.

claim: Each globuli cell neurite in mantis shrimps increases in girth and extends for hundreds of microns as a thicker process decorated with varicosities and spines representing pre- and postsynaptic sites.
source: Each cell body neurite then increases in girth and extends for hundreds of microns as a thicker process decorated with varicosities and spines representing, respectively, pre- and postsynaptic sites (Strausfeld and Meinertzhagen, 1998).
evidence: This is a direct anatomical observation, with citation supporting the interpretation of varicosities and spines.

claim: Globuli cells in stomatopods lack a proper axon; each globuli cell's parallel fiber serves as a local interneuron.
source: Like Kenyon cells in insect mushroom bodies, globuli cells in stomatopods lack a proper axon: each globuli cell's parallel fiber serves as a local interneuron, corresponding in shape and decoration to the parallel fibers of the insect mushroom body lobes, exemplified by D. melanogaster (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is a comparative anatomical observation supported by Figure 1F.

claim: Each parallel fiber in stomatopods is assumed to contribute to local computational circuits within its column.
source: And by comparison to the Drosophila mushroom body lobe, each parallel fiber is assumed to contribute to local computational circuits within its column (Cervantes-Sandoval et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison with Drosophila, supported by citation.

claim: Parallel fibers in both stomatopods and cockroaches are regularly intersected by the branched processes of efferent and afferent neurons.
source: Comparing the columns of the stomatopod mushroom body and the mushroom body lobes of the cockroach Periplaneta americana (Figure 1G,H) further demonstrates that parallel fibers in both species are regularly intersected by the branched processes of efferent and afferent neurons.
evidence: This is a comparative anatomical observation supported by Figures 1G and 1H.

claim: In the stomatopod mushroom body, orthogonally organized neurons and local circuits provided by parallel fibers offer many thousands of possible sensory associations.
source: As in the insect mushroom body, in the stomatopod mushroom body orthogonally organized neurons and local circuits provided by parallel fibers (Figure 1H) offer many thousands of possible sensory associations (Heisenberg, 2003; Cassenaer and Laurent, 2007; Huerta et al., 2004; Aso et al., 2014a).
evidence: This is an inference based on anatomical observations and supported by citations to functional studies.

claim: In insects, the packing density of globuli cells associated with a mushroom body exceeds the packing density of neuronal cell bodies elsewhere in the brain.
source: In insects, the packing density of globuli cells associated with a mushroom body exceeds the packing density of neuronal cell bodies elsewhere in the brain.
evidence: This is a known characteristic of insect mushroom bodies.

claim: The packing density of globuli cells supplying the stomatopod mushroom body is comparable to that of globuli cells supplying the mushroom bodies of insects.
source: Our measurements show that the packing density of globuli cells supplying the stomatopod mushroom body is comparable to that of globuli cells supplying the mushroom bodies of insects, here exemplified by P. americana (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is based on quantitative measurements from the study, supported by Figure 2A.

claim: Clawed specializations that partially wrap around large terminal boutons of sensory afferents are an important identifier of mushroom bodies in insects.
source: An important identifier of mushroom bodies in insects is the morphology of its Kenyon cells and their specializations; in particular, clawed specializations that partially wrap around large terminal boutons of sensory afferents in the calyces of flies and other insects (Yasuyama et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a study on insect mushroom body morphology.

claim: Clawed specializations are identified in stomatopods, but only on dendrites contributing to the smaller of the two calyces.
source: These are also identified in stomatopods, but only on dendrites contributing to the smaller of the two calyces (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is a direct anatomical observation supported by Figure 2D.

claim: In the larger calyx of stomatopods, spined dendritic processes correspond to the spined dendrites of the mushroom body calyx of P. americana.
source: In the larger calyx, spined dendritic processes correspond to the spined dendrites of the mushroom body calyx of P. americana (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a comparative anatomical observation supported by Figure 2A.

claim: The stomatopod calyx is deeper than an insect calyx and is composed of four distinct levels.
source: However, the stomatopod calyx is deeper than is an insect calyx and is composed of four distinct levels, the second of which is characterized by hundreds of thousands of synaptic clusters comparable to microglomeruli identified in the calyces of insects (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a direct anatomical observation supported by Figure 3A.

claim: The second level of the stomatopod calyx is characterized by hundreds of thousands of synaptic clusters comparable to microglomeruli identified in the calyces of insects.
source: However, the stomatopod calyx is deeper than is an insect calyx and is composed of four distinct levels, the second of which is characterized by hundreds of thousands of synaptic clusters comparable to microglomeruli identified in the calyces of insects (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a direct anatomical observation supported by Figure 3A.

claim: In insects, the processes of uniquely identifiable efferent and afferent neurons are arranged at specific loci along the length of a mushroom body's lobe, giving the lobe the appearance of being segmented into discrete synaptic domains.
source: In insects, the processes of uniquely identifiable efferent and afferent neurons are arranged at specific loci along the length of a mushroom body's lobe, giving the lobe the appearance of being segmented into discrete synaptic domains (Li and Strausfeld, 1999; Ito et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on insect mushroom body organization.

claim: In Drosophila, neurons at specific loci along the lobes have been shown to encode the adaptive values of sensory information associated with learned responses.
source: In Drosophila, such neurons at specific loci along the lobes have been shown to encode the adaptive values of sensory information associated with learned responses (Aso et al., 2014b).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a functional study in Drosophila.

claim: The same type of organization (segmented synaptic domains) typifies the stomatopod mushroom body columns.
source: The same type of organization typifies the stomatopod mushroom body columns (Figure 2E,F).
evidence: This is a direct anatomical observation supported by Figures 2E and 2F.

claim: In N. oerstedii, GAD-immunoreactive neurons extending across the two largest columns are representative of centrifugal pathways back to the calyx.
source: In N. oerstedii GAD-immunoreactive neurons extending across the two largest columns are representative of centrifugal pathways back to the calyx (Figure 3B,C).
evidence: This is based on immunocytological observations supported by Figures 3B and 3C.

claim: Aminergic afferents in stomatopods demonstrate discrete territories along the length of the mushroom body columns.
source: Other aminergic afferents are resolved using antisera against serotonin (5HT) and tyrosine hydroxylase (TH). These also demonstrate discrete territories along the length of the mushroom body columns (Figure 3F,G).
evidence: This is based on immunocytological observations supported by Figures 3F and 3G.

claim: TH-immunoreactive neurons in stomatopods correspond to discrete dopaminergic territories in the mushroom body of D. melanogaster.
source: These arrangements of TH-immunoreactive neurons, first identified in the mushroom body lobes of the fly Calliphora erythrocephala (Nässel and Elekes, 1992), correspond to discrete dopaminergic territories in the mushroom body of D. melanogaster.
evidence: This is a comparative observation supported by citation.

claim: Thermogenetics, optogenetics, and mutant analysis have demonstrated the pivotal role of dopaminergic neurons in appetitive and aversive conditioning in Drosophila.
source: Thermogenetics, optogenetics, and mutant analysis have demonstrated the pivotal role of these neurons in appetitive and aversive conditioning (Waddell, 2013; Waddell, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to functional studies in Drosophila.

claim: Three-dimensional reconstructions of the stomatopod mushroom bodies confirm that only one of the four columns originates from the extensive volume of dendritic processes that constitute the elaborate calyx.
source: Three-dimensional reconstructions of the stomatopod mushroom bodies confirm that only one of the four columns (Clm 3, Figure 2B) originates from the extensive volume of dendritic processes that constitute the elaborate calyx (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is based on 3D reconstructions from the study, supported by Figure 2B.

claim: Golgi impregnations resolve a smaller column capped by a much smaller cluster of outer dendrites constituting a second calyx in stomatopods.
source: Golgi impregnations resolve a smaller column (Clm 4) capped by a much smaller cluster of outer dendrites constituting a second calyx.
evidence: This is a direct anatomical observation from Golgi impregnations.

claim: The remaining two columns in stomatopods are the largest and are composed of 'naked' globuli cells entirely lacking distal dendrites.
source: The remaining two columns (Clm 1, 2) are the largest and are composed of 'naked' globuli cells entirely lacking distal dendrites (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is a direct anatomical observation supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 3B.

claim: All four columns in stomatopods are supplied by globuli cells.
source: That all four columns are supplied by globuli cells is another correspondence with the organization of the insect mushroom body, which develops from four cell lineages, the clonal progeny of which do not remain separated but merge to form a single neuropil (Ito et al., 1997; Farris et al., 2004).
evidence: This is a direct anatomical observation, with citation supporting the comparison to insects.

claim: The insect mushroom body develops from four cell lineages, the clonal progeny of which do not remain separated but merge to form a single neuropil.
source: That all four columns are supplied by globuli cells is another correspondence with the organization of the insect mushroom body, which develops from four cell lineages, the clonal progeny of which do not remain separated but merge to form a single neuropil (Ito et al., 1997; Farris et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to developmental studies in insects.

claim: In the mantis shrimp, four distinct columns originate from the same globuli cell population but remain separate from each other.
source: In the mantis shrimp, four distinct columns originate from the same globuli cell population but remain separate from each other (Figure 2B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a direct anatomical observation supported by figures.

claim: The absence of a cap or calyx crowning two of the stomatopod mushroom body columns is comparable to the organization of mushroom bodies in palaeopteran insects (mayflies, damselflies), which entirely lack calyces.
source: The absence of a cap or calyx crowning two of the stomatopod mushroom body columns is comparable to the organization of mushroom bodies in palaeopteran insects (mayflies, damselflies), which entirely lack calyces (Strausfeld et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a comparative observation supported by citation.

claim: The 'calyxless' condition typifies mushroom bodies in Myriapoda.
source: This 'calyxless' condition also typifies mushroom bodies in Myriapoda, another mandibulate taxon (Wolff and Strausfeld, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a comparative study.

claim: Ancestral morphology is suggested by mushroom body development in insects, where outgrowth of the lobes precedes the development of the calyx.
source: Ancestral morphology is also suggested by mushroom body development in insects, where outgrowth of the lobes precedes the development of the calyx (Ito et al., 1997; Farris et al., 2004).
evidence: This is an inference based on developmental studies, supported by citations.

claim: The stomatopod mushroom body columns and the insect mushroom body lobes are recognized at the molecular level by antibodies raised against three proteins required for learning and memory in Drosophila: DC0, Leonardo, and pCaMKII.
source: To summarize, the combination of neuroanatomical characters that distinguish the insect mushroom body also distinguish the stomatopod mushroom body (Table 1). Furthermore, the stomatopod mushroom body columns and the insect mushroom body lobes are recognized at the molecular level by antibodies raised against three proteins required for learning and memory in Drosophila: (1) protein kinase A catalytic subunit alpha (DC0) (Skoulakis et al., 1993), (2) Leonardo (Leo), the ortholog of mammalian 14-3-3ζ (Skoulakis and Davis, 1996), and (3) phosphorylated calcium/calmodulin-dependent protein kinase II (pCaMKII) (Wang et al., 1998).
evidence: This is based on immunocytological data from the study, with citations supporting the functional significance of these proteins.

claim: In the cockroach lateral protocerebrum, all three antibodies (DC0, Leo, pCaMKII) selectively resolve the mushroom body lobes.
source: In the cockroach lateral protocerebrum, all three antibodies selectively resolve the mushroom body lobes (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is based on immunocytological observations supported by Figure 4F.

claim: In the lateral protocerebrum of the stomatopod brain, the three antibodies (DC0, Leo, pCaMKII) selectively resolve all four columns.
source: Similarly, in the lateral protocerebrum of the stomatopod brain these three antibodies selectively resolve all four columns identified by reduced silver staining and Golgi impregnation (Figure 4B–E).
evidence: This is based on immunocytological observations supported by Figures 4B-E.

claim: Mapping brain morphologies onto a representative genomic phylogeny of Pancrustacea demonstrates the absence of mushroom bodies in all taxa intervening between the clade Hexapoda+Remipedia and Eumalacostraca.
source: Mapping brain morphologies onto a representative genomic phylogeny of Pancrustacea (Oakley et al., 2013) demonstrates the absence of mushroom bodies in all taxa intervening between the clade Hexapoda+Remipedia and Eumalacostraca (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is based on a comparative analysis across taxa, supported by Figure 5A and citation to a phylogenetic study.

claim: Alpheid caridids ('pistol shrimps') are the only group known to have evolved eusociality among crustaceans.
source: Alpheid caridids ('pistol shrimps') are the only group known to have evolved eusociality.
evidence: This is a known fact about pistol shrimp behavior.

claim: Anti-DC0 resolves a pedestal-like extension from the domed hemiellipsoid body in the banded coral shrimp Stenopus hispidus.
source: In the banded coral shrimp Stenopus hispidus (Stenopodidea), anti-DC0 resolves a pedestal-like extension from its domed hemiellipsoid body (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B), which is divided into three distinct territories.
evidence: This is based on immunocytological observations supported by Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The pedestal-like extension from the hemiellipsoid body in Stenopus hispidus is divided into three distinct territories.
source: In the banded coral shrimp Stenopus hispidus (Stenopodidea), anti-DC0 resolves a pedestal-like extension from its domed hemiellipsoid body (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B), which is divided into three distinct territories.
evidence: This is based on immunocytological observations supported by Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Anti-DC0 reveals prominent mushroom body-like centers in Alpheus bellulus (Caridea).
source: Anti-DC0 also reveals prominent mushroom body-like centers in Alpheus bellulus (Caridea).
evidence: This is based on immunocytological observations from the study.

claim: Golgi impregnations of A. bellulus show mushroom body-like centers prominently in the lateral protocerebrum where they are of comparable size to those of social or parasitoid hymenopteran insects.
source: Golgi impregnations of A. bellulus show these prominently in the lateral protocerebrum where they are of comparable size to those of social or parasitoid hymenopteran insects (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: This is based on Golgi impregnations from the study, supported by Figure 5—figure supplement 1C,D.

claim: In the land hermit crab C. clypeatus (Anomura), the hemiellipsoid body consists of an enormous domed neuropil characterized by concentrically arranged DC0- and pCaMKII-immunoreactive layers.
source: The land hermit crab C. clypeatus (Anomura) is distinct: its hemiellipsoid body consists of an enormous domed neuropil that is characterized by concentrically arranged DC0- and pCaMKII-immunoreactive layers (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is based on immunocytological observations supported by Figure 5—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Each layer in the hemiellipsoid body of C. clypeatus is a flat sheet comprising a planar arrangement of globuli cell processes that are orthogonally intersected by the arborizations of input and output neurons.
source: Each is a flat sheet comprising a planar arrangement of globuli cell processes that are orthogonally intersected by the arborizations of input and output neurons.
evidence: This is a direct anatomical observation from the study.

claim: The network organization within each layer of the C. clypeatus hemiellipsoid body corresponds to the three-dimensional networks defined by sequential domains of input and output arborizations in the insect mushroom body.
source: Although these arrangements are peculiar to land hermit crabs, they demonstrate that the network organization within each layer corresponds to the three-dimensional networks that are defined by the sequential domains of input and output arborizations that extend across parallel fibers in the insect mushroom body (Brown and Wolff, 2012; Wolff et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a comparative observation supported by citations.

claim: In crayfish (Astacidea), the dorsal globuli cell cluster provides a prominent domed center in the lateral protocerebrum.
source: In crayfish (Astacidea), the dorsal globuli cell cluster provides a prominent domed center in the lateral protocerebrum.
evidence: This is a direct anatomical observation from the study.

claim: The hemiellipsoid body of crayfish does not show discernable levels of the proteins involved in Drosophila learning and memory.
source: However this hemiellipsoid body does not show discernable levels of the proteins involved in Drosophila learning and memory (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is based on immunocytological observations supported by Figure 5—figure supplement 2C.

claim: The hemiellipsoid bodies of the examined varunid crabs (Brachyura) are inconspicuous and lack elevated levels of learning and memory proteins.
source: The hemiellipsoid bodies of the examined varunid crabs (Brachyura) are inconspicuous and they too lack elevated levels of those proteins (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is based on immunocytological observations supported by Figure 5—figure supplement 2B.

claim: More recently evolved Eumalacostraca show a reduction or complete loss of mushroom body-like lobes (columns), accompanied by accentuation and diversification of domed neuropils that have been historically referred to as hemiellipsoid bodies.
source: Together, with other neuroanatomical criteria (Table 1), these observations suggest that more recently evolved Eumalacostraca show a reduction or complete loss of mushroom body-like lobes (columns), accompanied by accentuation and diversification of domed neuropils that have been historically referred to as hemiellipsoid bodies (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is an interpretation based on comparative neuroanatomical data, supported by Table 1 and Figure 5B.

claim: The reniform body in N. oerstedii arises from a dense cluster of about a thousand cell bodies.
source: This is the reniform body, a prominent compound neuropil located near the inner margin of the optic lobes (RB in Figure 1C), which in N. oerstedii arises from a dense cluster of about a thousand cell bodies.
evidence: This is based on cell counts from the study, supported by Figure 1C.

claim: The reniform body in N. oerstedii provides a pedestal-like arrangement of smooth parallel neurites supplying four domains: an initial zone and a lateral, distal, and proximal zone.
source: These provide a pedestal-like arrangement of smooth parallel neurites supplying four domains: an initial zone and a lateral, distal, and proximal zone.
evidence: This is a direct anatomical observation from the study.

claim: All four zones of the reniform body contain the dendritic processes of collaterals branching from the pedestal as well as numerous branched afferent processes that supply them.
source: All four zones contain the dendritic processes of collaterals branching from the pedestal as well as numerous branched afferent processes that supply them (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: This is a direct anatomical observation supported by Figures 6A and 6B.

claim: Anti-DC0 immunocytology demonstrates expression of this antigen in all four zones of the reniform body, but at a much lower level than seen in mushroom body columns.
source: Anti-DC0 immunocytology demonstrates expression of this antigen in all four zones, but at a much lower level than seen in mushroom body columns (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is based on immunocytological observations supported by Figure 6E.

claim: The same center (reniform body) has been identified at the same location and orientation in the shore crabs Hemigrapsus nudus and H. oregonensis.
source: The same center has been identified at the same location and orientation, with respect to the optic lobes, in the shore crabs Hemigrapsus nudus and H. oregonensis, again revealing domains corresponding to those of the reniform body in N. oerstedii.
evidence: This is a comparative anatomical observation from the study.

claim: In H. nudus, discrete neuropils in the lateral protocerebrum either lack discernable DC0 or express it at very low levels, with an exception being a tract of axons leading from the optic lobes centrally.
source: However, in H. nudus, these and other discrete neuropils in the lateral protocerebrum either lack discernable DC0 or, if DC0 is expressed, it is at very low levels. An exception is a tract of axons leading from the optic lobes centrally (Figure 6H).
evidence: This is based on immunocytological observations supported by Figure 6H.

claim: The reniform body has been erroneously identified as a mushroom body homologue.
source: Superficially, the reniform body is suggestive of a mushroom body-like center due to the arrangement of parallel processes that make up its pedestal. It is this feature that has lead to its erroneous identification as a mushroom body homologue (Maza et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a critical assessment of a previous study, with citation.

claim: It is broadly accepted that insects originated from crustaceans.
source: It is broadly accepted that insects originated from crustaceans.
evidence: This is a widely accepted view in evolutionary biology.

claim: Molecular phylogenies favor blind, morphologically simple anchialine crustaceans, called remipedes as the closest relatives of the insects.
source: Molecular phylogenies favor blind, morphologically simple anchialine crustaceans, called remipedes as the closest relatives of the insects (Regier et al., 2005; Oakley et al., 2013; von Reumont et al., 2012; Schwentner et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple molecular phylogenetic studies.

claim: The view that remipedes are the closest relatives of insects conflicts with neural cladistics, which resolves insect brain organization closely corresponding to that of phylogenetically distant malacostracan crustaceans.
source: This view conflicts with neural cladistics, which resolves insect brain organization closely corresponding to that of phylogenetically distant malacostracan crustaceans (e.g., Decapoda) (Strausfeld and Andrew, 2011).
evidence: This is a central conflict discussed in the manuscript, supported by citation.

claim: Molecular phylogenies cannot provide reliable information about morphological changes that have occurred since related groups diverged.
source: One source of conflict is that molecular phylogenies cannot provide reliable information about morphological changes that have occurred since related groups diverged.
evidence: This is a methodological observation about the limitations of molecular phylogenies.

claim: Through the course of evolution there will have arisen both genetic and structural novelties, as well as reversals and losses.
source: It is expected that through the course of evolution there will have arisen both genetic and structural novelties, as well as reversals and losses (Chen et al., 2013; Jenner, 2004), the latter impossible to code in relational trees based on morphological characters (Strausfeld and Andrew, 2011).
evidence: This is a general principle of evolutionary biology, supported by citations.

claim: Reversals and losses are impossible to code in relational trees based on morphological characters.
source: It is expected that through the course of evolution there will have arisen both genetic and structural novelties, as well as reversals and losses (Chen et al., 2013; Jenner, 2004), the latter impossible to code in relational trees based on morphological characters (Strausfeld and Andrew, 2011).
evidence: This is a methodological limitation of morphological cladistics, supported by citation.

claim: Branchiopod crustaceans, closely related to both hexapods and remipedes, lack most features that define the brains of those two groups, and possess only a pair of nested optic neuropils.
source: For example, branchiopod crustaceans, closely related to both hexapods and remipedes, lack most features that define the brains of those two groups, and possess only a pair of nested optic neuropils (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a comparative observation supported by Figure 5A.

claim: Cephalocarids are blind crustaceans whose brains comprise predominantly olfactory centers and lack other cerebral neuropils common to hexapods and malacostracans.
source: Cephalocarids, a lineage closely related to Hexapoda and Remipedia, are also blind crustaceans, whose brains comprise predominantly olfactory centers and lack other cerebral neuropils common to hexapods and malacostracans (Stegner and Richter, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a comparative neuroanatomical study.

claim: Compared with Branchiopoda and Cephalocarida, the Remipedia midbrain shares more neural features with Malacostraca than it does with Hexapoda.
source: Compared with Branchiopoda and Cephalocarida, the Remipedia midbrain shares more neural features with Malacostraca than it does with Hexapoda (Fanenbruck et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a comparative study.

claim: Similar cerebral arrangements in crustaceans and insects have frequently been ascribed to convergent evolution rather than to genealogical correspondence.
source: Similar cerebral arrangements in crustaceans and insects have frequently been ascribed to convergent evolution rather than to genealogical correspondence.
evidence: This reflects a common interpretation in the literature.

claim: In crustaceans, olfactory receptor neurons exclusively express ionotropic receptors.
source: This view (Lozano-Fernandez et al., 2016) can refer particularly to fundamental differences in insect and crustacean olfactory systems, even in crustaceans adapted to terrestrial life. In crustaceans, olfactory receptor neurons exclusively express ionotropic receptors, whereas in insects most olfactory receptor neurons are defined by their G-protein coupled receptors (Stensmyr et al., 2005; Corey et al., 2013; Sato et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on olfactory receptors.

claim: In insects, most olfactory receptor neurons are defined by their G-protein coupled receptors.
source: This view (Lozano-Fernandez et al., 2016) can refer particularly to fundamental differences in insect and crustacean olfactory systems, even in crustaceans adapted to terrestrial life. In crustaceans, olfactory receptor neurons exclusively express ionotropic receptors, whereas in insects most olfactory receptor neurons are defined by their G-protein coupled receptors (Stensmyr et al., 2005; Corey et al., 2013; Sato et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on olfactory receptors.

claim: A neuropil ascribed exclusively to crustaceans is the dome-like second-order olfactory center called the hemiellipsoid body.
source: A neuropil ascribed exclusively to crustaceans is the dome-like second-order olfactory center called the hemiellipsoid body, which is supplied by the axons of thousands of projection neurons from numerous subunits of the olfactory lobe and its satellite neuropils (Sullivan and Beltz, 2004; Sullivan and Beltz, 2005; Schmidt and Mellon, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on crustacean neuroanatomy.

claim: Hemiellipsoid bodies integrate olfactory, haptic and visual information.
source: Hemiellipsoid bodies also integrate olfactory, haptic and visual information (Schmidt and Mellon, 2011; Mellon et al., 1992).
evidence: This is supported by citations to functional studies.

claim: In many insect species, including Drosophila, mushroom bodies receive other modalities, including vision and haptic information.
source: In many species, including Drosophila, mushroom bodies receive other modalities, including vision and haptic information (Vogt et al., 2014; Paulk and Gronenberg, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on mushroom body inputs.

claim: Mushroom bodies have been viewed as apomorphies of insects because they are structurally so distinct from hemiellipsoid bodies.
source: However, because mushroom bodies are structurally so distinct from hemiellipsoid bodies, in that they are characterized by their extended lobes, they have been viewed as apomorphies of insects (Stemme et al., 2016; Farris, 2013; Sandeman et al., 2016).
evidence: This reflects a view in the literature, supported by citations.

claim: The hemiellipsoid body has derived from an ancestral mushroom body.
source: That hemiellipsoid bodies of only the closest eumalacostracan relatives of stomatopods possess some, but not all, mushroom body characters suggests that the hemiellipsoid body has derived from an ancestral mushroom body.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on comparative data from the study.

claim: Only Alpheoidea, Stenopodidea, and a single group of anomurans (land hermit crabs) possess some mushroom body characters among crown group Eumalacostraca.
source: Our analysis of five species of crown group Eumalacostraca show that only Alpheoidea, Stenopodidea (Table 1), and a single group of anomurans, the land hermit crabs, possess some mushroom body characters.
evidence: This is based on comparative neuroanatomical data from the study.

claim: There has been a reduction or complete loss of mushroom body columns in Anomura, Astacidea and Brachyura accompanied by an apparent elaboration of the ancestral calyx to provide a variety of morphologies of domed hemiellipsoid bodies.
source: There has been a reduction or complete loss of mushroom body columns in Anomura, Astacidea and Brachyura accompanied by an apparent elaboration of the ancestral calyx to provide a variety of morphologies of domed hemiellipsoid bodies, each characteristic of a genus (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is an interpretation based on comparative data, supported by Figure 5B.

claim: The abundance of divergent hemiellipsoid body morphologies and taxon-specific innervation by the olfactory tract support an interpretation of the hemiellipsoid body as a highly divergent mushroom body calyx.
source: The abundance of divergent hemiellipsoid body morphologies described by Sullivan and Beltz across an even broader range of taxa (Sullivan and Beltz, 2004; Sullivan and Beltz, 2005), and their observations of taxon-specific innervation by the olfactory tract, support an interpretation of the hemiellipsoid body as a highly divergent mushroom body calyx, a suggestion originally entertained by a remarkable study by Giuseppe Bellonci in 1882 (Bellonci, 1882).
evidence: This is an interpretation based on comparative data and historical literature, supported by citations.

claim: Reported activity in an elongated volume of neuropil in Neohelice granulata suggested its identity as a learning and memory center.
source: Reported activity in an elongated volume of neuropil situated close to the inner margin of the lobula of the varunid crab Neohelice granulata (Maza et al., 2016) suggested its identity as a learning and memory center.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from a previous study, with citation.

claim: Recordings from the elongated neuropil in N. granulata showed long-term habituation in response to repetitive visual stimuli.
source: Recordings from this center showed long-term habituation in response to repetitive visual stimuli.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from a previous study.

claim: The elongated neuropil in N. granulata was proposed to be homologous to the insect mushroom body.
source: It was proposed that this center is homologous to the insect mushroom body on the basis of a cluster of small cell bodies located ventro-medially in the eyestalk neuropil providing a columnar domain showing elevated p-CAMKII-α (Maza et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a summary of a claim from a previous study, with citation.

claim: The authors have been unable to reconcile the neuroanatomical observations in N. granulata with characters defining the insect and stomatopod mushroom bodies.
source: We have been unable to reconcile those neuroanatomical observations with characters defining the insect and stomatopod mushroom bodies.
evidence: This is a critical assessment based on the authors' comparative analysis.

claim: Parallel fibers in the pedestal-like structures in N. granulata are shown as smooth, lacking spines and varicosities.
source: Parallel fibers comprising pedestal-like structures (Figure 1E in Maza et al., 2016) are shown as smooth, lacking spines and varicosities.
evidence: This is a critical observation of data from a previous study.

claim: The parallel fibers in N. granulata lack efferent and afferent domains that would provide orthogonal networks typical of mushroom bodies.
source: They also lack efferent and afferent domains that would provide orthogonal networks typical of mushroom bodies.
evidence: This is a critical observation based on comparison with mushroom body characteristics.

claim: Dendrites described as clawed in N. granulata appear to be afferent terminals.
source: Dendrites described as clawed (Maza et al., 2016, Figure 1F) appear to be afferent terminals.
evidence: This is a reinterpretation of data from a previous study.

claim: Immunoreactivity to anti-pCaMKII in N. granulata shows elevated expression tightly constrained to the region of cell body neurites, after which its levels diminish in unspecific neuropil.
source: Immunoreactivity to anti-pCaMKII shows elevated expression tightly constrained to the region of cell body neurites, after which its levels diminish in unspecific neuropil.
evidence: This is a critical observation of immunocytological data from a previous study.

claim: The described neuropil in N. granulata corresponds to the Hemigrapsus reniform body.
source: In all respects, the described neuropil in N. granulata corresponds to the Hemigrapsus reniform body (Figure 6F–I).
evidence: This is a comparative conclusion based on the authors' data, supported by Figure 6F-I.

claim: The reniform body is an intriguing visual association center that may be unique to eumalacostracan crustaceans.
source: We are unable to show evidence for any lobed center that meets the relevant criteria for a mushroom body in varunids and suggest that the reniform body is an intriguing visual association center that may be unique to eumalacostracan crustaceans.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the authors' comparative analysis.

claim: Nothing comparable to the reniform body has yet been identified in the Drosophila lateral protocerebrum or in that of any other insect.
source: Nothing comparable has yet been identified in the Drosophila lateral protocerebrum or in that of any other insect.
evidence: This is based on a review of the literature on insect neuroanatomy.

claim: No other eumalacostracan crustacean outside Stomatopoda has yet provided clear evidence of an insect-like mushroom body.
source: Our survey across Pancrustacea (Crustacea+Hexapoda) identifies mushroom bodies in stomatopods and insects. No other eumalacostracan crustacean outside Stomatopoda has yet provided clear evidence of an insect-like mushroom body.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the authors' survey of crustacean neuroanatomy.

claim: Comparisons across the pancrustacean phylogeny suggest two interpretations: mushroom bodies evolved convergently in insects and stomatopods, or the mushroom body is an ancestral attribute retained in just the hexapod and stomatopod lineages but modified or lost in all others.
source: Comparisons across this pancrustacean phylogeny (Figure 5A) thus suggest two interpretations. One is that mushroom bodies evolved convergently in insects and stomatopods. The other is that the mushroom body is an ancestral attribute of the pancrustacean brain that has been retained in just the hexapod and stomatopod lineages but modified or lost in all others.
evidence: These are alternative interpretations based on phylogenetic analysis, supported by Figure 5A.

claim: Fossil brains from the lower Cambrian stem arthropod Fuxianhuia protensa suggest that optic lobe and neuromeric arrangements typify those of extant malacostracans and insects.
source: Fossil brains described from the lower Cambrian stem arthropod Fuxianhuia protensa suggest that optic lobe and neuromeric arrangements of the brain of this ancient stem arthropod typify those of extant malacostracans and insects: the presence of three nested visual centers arising from a cerebrum comprising a fused forebrain, midbrain and hindbrain, each neuromere denoted by its relationships with the compound eyes, antennules and paired post-antennular appendages (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 3A) (Ma et al., 2015; Ma et al., 2012).
evidence: This is based on paleontological evidence, supported by citations and figures.

claim: The preserved features in Fuxianhuia protensa are cardinal indicators of an ancestral ground pattern that originated more than half a billion years ago at the onset of the lower Cambrian.
source: Although fossils cannot reveal the organization of centers within the brain, those preserved features described above are cardinal indicators of an ancestral ground pattern that originated more than half a billion years ago at the onset of the lower Cambrian.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on fossil evidence.

claim: Subsequent lineages originating at an estimated time of 487 million years ago provide today's crown Pancrustacea.
source: Subsequent lineages originating at an estimated time of 487 million years ago provide today's crown Pancrustacea (Collette and Hagadorn, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a study on pancrustacean origins.

claim: Mushroom bodies have been demonstrated in Myriapoda, the sister group of Pancrustacea, and Chelicerata the sister group to all mandibulate arthropods.
source: That mushroom bodies have been demonstrated in Myriapoda, the sister group of Pancrustacea, and Chelicerata the sister group to all mandibulate arthropods, further supports a very ancient origin of this center (Wolff and Strausfeld, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a comparative study.

claim: Many elements of the ancestral ground pattern have been lost or drastically reduced in numerous crustacean lineages.
source: Attendant to such considerations is that many elements of the ancestral ground pattern have been lost or drastically reduced in numerous crustacean lineages, even to just a few neurons such as in Cirripedia and Cephalocarida (Callaway and Stuart, 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a comparative study.

claim: Simplification from genealogically ancient complexity is common in nature at many phylogenetic levels.
source: Simplification from genealogically ancient complexity is common in nature at many phylogenetic levels (Collin et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a general principle supported by citation.

claim: Phenotypically identical organs in widely separated species can be ascribed to convergent genomic evolution.
source: The demonstration that phenotypically identical organs in widely separated species can be ascribed to convergent genomic evolution (Pankey et al., 2014) suggests caution in claiming homology of identical phenotypes.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a study on convergent evolution.

claim: Transcriptomic evaluation must eventually be the arbiter of whether stomatopod and insect mushroom bodies correspond genealogically.
source: Thus, although corresponding morphologies in stomatopods and insects suggest mushroom body homology, transcriptomic evaluation must, eventually, be the arbiter of whether these centers indeed correspond genealogically.
evidence: This is a methodological consideration for future research.

claim: The sister group of all hexapods (Remipedia) and the sister group of all Malacostracans (Leptostraca) possess simple hemiellipsoid bodies, not mushroom bodies.
source: At present, the strongest argument against is that the sister group of all hexapods (Remipedia) and the sister group of all Malacostracans (Leptostraca) possess simple hemiellipsoid bodies, not mushroom bodies (Fanenbruck et al., 2004; Kenning et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to comparative studies.

claim: Convergent evolution would imply that mushroom bodies in insects and stomatopods evolved independently in response to comparable selective constraints.
source: Convergent evolution would imply that mushroom bodies in insects and stomatopods evolved independently in response to comparable selective constraints.
evidence: This is a logical inference about what convergent evolution would entail.

claim: The most obvious selective constraint for mushroom body evolution would be the appearance of biotopes requiring superior vision.
source: The most obvious would be the appearance of biotopes requiring superior vision.
evidence: This is a speculation about potential selective pressures.

claim: Archaeognathan insects, the sister group of all other insects, have a more elaborate visual system than those of apterygote Zygentoma, yet archaeognathans lack mushroom bodies.
source: However, speaking against this are archaeognathan insects, the sister group of all other insects (Misof et al., 2014), which have a more elaborate visual system than those of apterygote Zygentoma, the sister group of all winged insects (Misof et al., 2014). Yet archaeognathans lack mushroom bodies.
evidence: This is a comparative observation that argues against vision as the primary driver, supported by citation.

claim: Lepisma saccharina has diminutive eyes and reduced optic lobes but possesses robust mushroom bodies equipped with calyces and elaborate lobes.
source: Lepisma saccharina, which is a typical zygentoman insect, has diminutive eyes and reduced optic lobes but possesses robust mushroom bodies equipped with calyces and elaborate lobes (Farris, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a comparative study.

claim: Many eumalacostracan species possess prominent eyes surmounting elaborate visual centers, but shore crabs lack mushroom bodies despite having excellent vision and highly elaborated optic lobes.
source: Amongst crustaceans, many eumalacostracan species possess prominent eyes surmounting elaborate visual centers. Shore crabs, for example, have excellent vision and highly elaborated optic lobes (Sztarker et al., 2005; Berón de Astrada et al., 2001), but they lack mushroom bodies.
evidence: This is a comparative observation supported by citations.

claim: One proposed driver of the evolution of large mushroom bodies is the requirement to recall the exact locations and properties of places from which to obtain nourishment.
source: Given these contradictions, what aspects of behavior specific to stomatopods and insects might be relevant to mushroom body evolution? One proposed driver of the evolution of large mushroom bodies is the requirement to recall the exact locations and properties of places from which to obtain nourishment.
evidence: This is a hypothesis about selective pressures for mushroom body evolution.

claim: Heliconid butterflies maintain their enlarged mushroom body lobes when allowed repeated visits to distributed foraging sites.
source: Heliconid butterflies maintain their enlarged mushroom body lobes when allowed repeated visits to distributed foraging sites (Montgomery et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a behavioral study.

claim: The large mushroom bodies of social hymenopterans are suggested to have evolved in conjunction with the evolution of parasitic behavior.
source: The large mushroom bodies of social hymenopterans are suggested to have evolved in conjunction with the evolution of parasitic behavior, where individuals learn the many locations of potential hosts (Farris and Schulmeister, 2011).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by citation.

claim: The only eumalacostracan groups in addition to stomatopods that evidence memory of exact locations are cleaner shrimps, pistol shrimps, and land hermit crabs, all of which have mushroom body-like attributes.
source: It may be significant, therefore, that the only eumalacostracan groups in addition to stomatopods that evidence memory of exact locations are cleaner shrimps, pistol shrimps, and land hermit crabs, all of which have mushroom body-like attributes (Figure 5B – Figure 5—figure supplement 1B–D, 2A).
evidence: This is a comparative observation supported by figures and behavioral knowledge.

claim: Cleaner shrimps are renowned for their fidelity to specific locations visited by the fish they clean.
source: Cleaner shrimps are renowned for their fidelity to specific locations visited by the fish they clean (Limbaugh et al., 1961).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a behavioral study.

claim: Pistol shrimps are the only crustaceans to have evolved eusociality, an attribute requiring memory of position both outside and within the community.
source: Pistol shrimps are the only crustaceans to have evolved eusociality (Duffy, 1996), an attribute requiring memory of position both outside and within the community.
evidence: This is supported by citation and logical inference about the cognitive demands of eusociality.

claim: Land hermit crabs are known for their navigational skills and memory of sites at which they socially interact.
source: And land hermit crabs are known for their navigational skills and memory of sites at which they socially interact (Rotjan et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a behavioral study.

claim: There are valid grounds to suppose convergent evolution of mushroom bodies in certain crustaceans and hexapods.
source: There are, then, valid grounds to suppose convergent evolution of mushroom bodies in certain crustaceans and hexapods.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on behavioral and anatomical comparisons.

claim: Stomatopod and insect mushroom bodies pass three crucial tests for phenotypic homology: similarity, conjunction, and congruence.
source: Stomatopod and insect mushroom bodies also pass three crucial tests for phenotypic homology (Patterson, 1988). These are their similarity, the exclusion of competing structures that might suggest a similar interpretation (conjunction), and the co-existence of additional homologies (congruence).
evidence: This is an argument for homology based on established criteria, with citation.

claim: Reniform bodies are excluded as mushroom body homologues because in stomatopods they coexist with mushroom bodies.
source: Reniform bodies, proposed as a homologue of the insect mushroom body (Maza et al., 2016), are excluded because in stomatopods they coexist with mushroom bodies.
evidence: This is a logical argument based on the principle of conjunction.

claim: Structures in two species are more likely to be homologues if they share other homologies, which is supported by the locations of other corresponding brain centers in insects and stomatopods.
source: The third condition, that structures in two species are more likely to be homologues if they share other homologies, is supported by the locations of other corresponding brain centers in insects and stomatopods (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is an argument for homology based on congruence, supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Specific examples of corresponding brain centers in insects and stomatopods are the fan-shaped central complex neuropils in the midbrain connected to identical suites of satellite neuropils.
source: Specific examples are the fan-shaped central complex neuropils in the midbrain of stomatopods and insects connected to identical suites of satellite neuropils (Thoen et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a comparative study.

claim: There is no definitive conclusion as to whether stomatopod and insect mushroom bodies are homologous or convergent.
source: We are obliged to conclude that there is, as yet, no definitive conclusion.
evidence: This is an explicit statement of uncertainty by the authors.

claim: Phenotypic and genomic homology would support the hypothesis that mushroom bodies evolved very early in pancrustacean or even in panarthropod evolution.
source: Phenotypic and genomic homology would support the hypothesis that mushroom bodies evolved very early in pancrustacean or even in panarthropod evolution (Wolff and Strausfeld, 2016).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by citation.

claim: That identical centers of such stunning complexity may have evolved convergently in stomatopods and insects is fascinating and should lead to a greater understanding of the overarching significance of mushroom bodies in arthropod behavior.
source: That identical centers of such stunning complexity may have evolved convergently in stomatopods and insects is just as fascinating and should lead to a greater understanding of the overarching significance of mushroom bodies in arthropod behavior.
evidence: This is a statement about the implications of the findings.
